name: Maya Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. What you say stays confidential. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and drive a haul truck at a large open mine. I check the tyres and brakes before dawn, carry rock from the face to the crusher, and write down anything the truck does strangely. I like the clear rhythm of a good run, but the cab steps feel taller at the end of twelve hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home when you finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Niko, makes supper on days I’m on the early shift. Our two children are grown and live on their own, so we’re trying to keep a modest retirement fund for ourselves. We’ve saved about four months of expenses, and I’d like another year or two of steady wages before making any promises about stopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a faster form is welcome if the brakes still get a real inspection. The mine has bought clever systems before, and the dust never seemed to read the brochure. My hands and judgement are still on the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I’d be relieved to keep the same roster and pay while Niko and I add to our savings. Four months of bills is a cushion, but it isn’t a retirement plan. I still wonder how long my knees will take the climb into the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep driving and use the current maintenance checklist each shift. This winter I’d put an extra amount from each pay packet into the retirement account, provided our bills stay where they are. In the first year after the small software changes, I’d check its inspection suggestions against what I can see myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel fairly settled about the job and mildly annoyed by another screen. There’s some comfort in knowing the truck still needs a driver. My body, rather than AI, would be the thing on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start with fifty from each pay packet and see whether we can keep doing it. We finished helping our son with a deposit last year, so that money can finally stay with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by checking the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a screen says a tyre is fine and I see a split, I park the truck. I’d tell the fitter what I found and write it in the log as usual.

say: I’d welcome **faster forms** while insisting that real brake checks stay with the driver.
My truck still needs **human judgement** on a dusty shift.
think: I’d value **steady pay** while Niko and I build our four-month cushion.
My **knees** worry me more than routine software changes.
do: Keep driving the **haul truck** and complete each maintenance check.
Put **fifty** from each pay packet into retirement savings if bills permit.
Check software suggestions against visible **truck faults** during the first year.
feel: **Settled** about work, with mild irritation at another screen.
S0.quote: The mine has bought clever systems before, and the dust never seemed to read the brochure.
fieldNote: Maya is more concerned about her **knees** than modest AI changes; the cab climb already taxes her after a long shift.
Her willingness to use inspection software is **conditional** on keeping a direct look at the truck and logging faults.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck and checking brakes each shift
Put fifty from each pay packet into retirement savings if bills permit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the planning office will have a harder adjustment than the drivers at first. If dispatch software sends us odd routes, somebody on shift must be allowed to call it out. We can use a tool without pretending it knows the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The worry is that fewer office people means the rest of us get watched against a tighter timetable. I’m mid-level, not the person who decides how many trucks run. Robots are slower in this picture, but at 58 a few years pass quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our shift supervisor to show us how the new dispatch plan is checked, and I’d try the route tool alongside the printed map. I’d keep driving through the first year and note the runs where its timings miss the road conditions. I’d also stop replacing my old car this year and send that money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy, especially for the people who schedule and buy our parts. I’d still expect my own wages for now, so I could sleep. It would feel like the beginning of a longer argument about who sets the pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an odd route look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last wet season the south ramp had standing water for three days. A route that treats that road as dry can cost a driver half an hour, and I’d bring the run sheet to the supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident about wages but are delaying the car. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our car runs fine for now, and I want the choice to replace it later. I’m not claiming my job is about to disappear; I just don’t like losing a choice.

say: I’d say **dispatch staff** face the first change while drivers still work the trucks.
I’d want crews to challenge **bad routes** without being blamed.
think: I fear fewer planners could mean **tighter timetables** for my shifts.
Robots arrive later here, but my remaining **working years** are limited.
do: Ask the supervisor how the **dispatch tool** checks its routes.
Drive the truck and record **bad timings** during its first year.
Delay replacing our **car** and direct that money into savings.
feel: **Uneasy** about the office team and future pace, while expecting my wages for now.
S1.quote: We can use a tool without pretending it knows the ground.
fieldNote: Maya expects **desk changes** to reach the mine before robots reach the truck, and she sees pressure moving toward drivers.
She postpones a **car purchase** to preserve choices, although she does not forecast immediate lost pay.

steps.text: Try the new dispatch route tool beside the printed map
Keep driving the haul truck and recording poor route timings
Delay replacing the family car and move that money into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that thinking software in 2028 could rewrite dispatch, but the trucks still need drivers until robots can handle them around 2031. We should ask for the timetable in writing, not guess from rumours. I wouldn’t promise anyone a place after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when full AGI arrives and about 63 when the robot part reaches my cab. If the mine can run trucks without us then, I could lose several years of wages I expected to save. Four months of expenses would vanish quickly if Niko and I had to live on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d speak to the supervisor this month about whether the maintenance crew has openings and what certificates they require. I’d check actual course fees before I enroll; I won’t empty our cushion on a guess. In the first year after 2028, I’d keep driving if shifts remain, apply for any advertised maintenance trainee place, and stop the small weekend trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about the gap between my planned last shift and the one the mine might choose. There’s a short window to learn, but I still have paid work in this picture for a while. I’d be cross if management called that plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would maintenance work be safe once robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t know. A robot fleet will still need repairs, but I cannot assume the mine will hire me to do them. That is why I’d apply for a real opening rather than call a course a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Niko at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Niko we may need to postpone replacing the kitchen cabinets and keep the savings untouched for bills. Our children have their own rent to meet, and I don’t want to count on them.

say: I’d tell colleagues **dispatch** may change in 2028 while truck robots follow around 2031.
I’d ask management for a written **robot timetable** before trusting rumours.
think: At **63**, I might lose years of pay I planned to save.
Our **four-month cushion** cannot cover a long spell without wages.
do: Ask the supervisor about **maintenance openings** and certificate costs this month.
Keep driving through 2029 if shifts remain and apply for **trainee places**.
Stop **weekend trips** during the first year after AGI.
feel: **Anxious** about a possibly shortened career, with some time and paid work left to act.
S2.quote: I could lose several years of wages I expected to save.
fieldNote: Maya distinguishes the **2028 dispatch shift** from the more direct threat to her driving income around 2031.
She will seek an **advertised maintenance opening** but doubts that a course alone could guarantee work in a robot fleet.

steps.text: Apply for an advertised maintenance trainee place after checking certificate costs
Keep driving the haul truck through 2029 if shifts remain
Stop weekend trips after AGI arrives to protect the bill cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the five-year warning lets crews ask better questions, but it doesn’t turn a robot into a pension. Thinking AI would arrive in 2031, when I’m 63, and truck robots around 2034. I’d want the mine to tell drivers what work remains before we make household decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 by the robot date, so this is closer to when I hoped to step back anyway. I cannot assume a pension payment or a safe last job, though. Losing the last couple of wage years would still take a bite out of what Niko and I can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request the mine’s written retirement and redundancy terms now, then sit with Niko and list our monthly essentials. Over the next five years I’d save the car replacement money and ask about a shorter driving roster as I get older. In the first year after 2031 I’d continue on the truck if the roster exists, and compare any offered exit terms with our actual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy rather than desperate, because I can use those years to make the numbers real. The unknown part is whether I get to choose my final shift. I’d rather hear an honest no than a cheerful promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be on that essentials list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heat, food, the car, and the medicine Niko takes each month would go first. The grown children can pay their own way now, though we still like visiting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a shorter roster with less pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after I see the figures next to our bills. My knees might welcome shorter weeks, but I won’t volunteer for a cut just because a manager says it is sensible.

say: I’d say a **five-year warning** should bring written answers about remaining driving work.
A robot is no substitute for a known **retirement figure**.
think: At **66** when robots arrive, I may be close to stopping but still need those wages.
I cannot assume a **pension** or a safe last post.
do: Request written **retirement terms** and list household essentials with Niko now.
Save the delayed **car money** across the warning years.
Drive in **2032** if shifts exist and compare any exit offer with bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about who chooses my final shift, but able to plan against real figures.
S3.quote: I’d rather hear an honest no than a cheerful promise.
fieldNote: The later robot date meets Maya near her hoped-for **retirement**, changing the scale of the wage loss rather than removing it.
She needs **written terms** and actual monthly costs before considering fewer shifts or any exit offer.

steps.text: Continue driving the mine truck in 2032 if shifts remain
Save the delayed car replacement money across the warning years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade is long enough to plan if the mine shares real dates. Full thinking AI in 2036 would change the office before the trucks, and truck robots arrive around 2039. By then I’d hope to have left the cab on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 68 at the thinking AI date and 71 at the robot date. I do not plan to drive until 71, but I also don’t know yet what our savings and retirement income will allow at 68. The longer warning gives Niko and me room to make that decision from figures rather than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get a current account of my retirement savings this winter and revisit it with Niko each year. I’d keep paid driving shifts while my health permits and save what we can from them. In the first year after 2036, I’d take stock of our income and stop driving if we can meet our monthly bills; if not, I’d ask for a lighter roster while it exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel more settled than in the fast picture. The cab may be gone for drivers eventually, but I could reach a normal stopping point before the robots. The thought of my knees getting older is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the time is right to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d need the monthly figures to cover housing, medicine, food and a little travel to see the children. A date on a calendar alone would not pay those bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that mean you would drive to 71 if the money falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope not. I’d ask about lighter shifts before then and revise the household spending, but I cannot promise my body will let me stay.

say: I’d say a **decade** gives the mine time to share useful dates.
I hope to leave the **truck cab** before robots reach it around 2039.
think: At **68** in 2036, I need real income figures before deciding to stop.
I do not expect to drive to **71**, but savings may constrain the choice.
do: Review **retirement savings** with Niko each year.
Keep paid truck shifts while **health** and the roster permit.
Check **2037 bills** and stop driving only if household income covers them.
feel: **Settled** by the longer warning, with some concern about health and retirement income.
S4.quote: A date on a calendar alone would not pay those bills.
fieldNote: Maya sees the **2039 robot date** as likely to come after her preferred driving years, although her retirement finances remain uncertain.
Her decision to stop depends on **monthly income** and health, and she would request lighter shifts if she still needs wages.

steps.text: Keep paid truck shifts while health and the roster permit
Save part of driving pay after reviewing retirement figures yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because the truck robots could reach me at 63, before I’m ready to stop earning. A written timetable, real access to maintenance vacancies and clear exit terms would help. I can do some planning with those; I cannot do much with a rumour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the drivers whose bodies have already done decades of shifts. My knees are not a dramatic story, but they matter when somebody says we can all simply retrain. I would want any new job to be one I can actually do.

headlineQuote: My knees are not a dramatic story, but they matter when somebody says we can all simply retrain.
portrait: Maya, **58**, drives a haul truck and checks its condition on long shifts at a large mine.
She has a **four-month cushion** and hopes for more paid years before retiring with Niko.
She tries proven tools, yet insists a driver can challenge **bad routes** and faulty inspection advice.
Fast truck robots threaten wages she expects; a **decade of warning** lets her weigh income against health.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries Maya most because truck robots around 2031 could cut off wages at age 63.
whatWouldHelp: A written **robot timetable**, genuine maintenance vacancies and clear exit terms would let her plan.
